items.title: Simulated, Real World, and Preferred Driving Styles: Passenger Perceptions of Robotaxi Aggressiveness and Trust
items.abstract: As Level 4 Robotaxis (RTs) transition into real-world deployment, understanding how passengers perceive driving behavior and form trust becomes increasingly critical. This study investigates the relationship between driving style, perceived aggressiveness, and trust across four urban driving scenarios using simulated RT videos. A total of 153 U.S. participants with prior RT experience evaluated simulated driving styles, their real-world counterparts, and their preferred styles. Results showed that perceived aggressiveness increased systematically with more aggressive driving styles and was significantly associated with decreased trust. Simulated driving styles at lower aggressiveness levels aligned closely with real-world perceptions, while higher levels deviated. Participants preferred more defensive driving styles than those perceived in real-world RTs. items.abstract: This article examines the relationship between metacognitive regulation and intrinsic motivation in developing students’ learning activity, with particular attention to the psychological mechanisms underlying their interaction. Metacognitive regulation is considered as a student’s ability to become aware of their own learning processes, plan educational activities, monitor their implementation, evaluate outcomes, and modify learning strategies when necessary. Intrinsic motivation refers to engagement in learning that is driven primarily by interest in knowledge, the desire to develop competence, and the personal meaning attributed to educational activities rather than by external rewards or pressure. The article highlights the contribution of goal setting, self-monitoring, reflection, attention regulation, independent decision-making, and academic persistence to students’ active participation in learning. It is also argued that an educational environment that supports learner autonomy, encourages reflective activities, provides opportunities for self-assessment, and allows students to select appropriate learning strategies can strengthen both metacognitive regulation and intrinsic motivation. The findings indicate that systematic development of these psychological resources can contribute to students’ formation as active, conscious, and responsible participants in the educational process.

items.title: Teacher and parental support as predictors of higher vocational college students’ academic performance: the mediating role of learning engagement
items.abstract: Drawing on social support theory, self-determination theory, and engagement theory, this study examines how teacher and parental support relate to academic performance in Chinese higher vocational colleges through learning engagement. This is one of the few studies in this context that integrates teacher support, parental support, and learning engagement in a single mediation model, clarifying how school- and home-based support systems work together to shape students’ academic performance. Together, these theories suggest that external support enhances performance primarily through engagement, which leads to the proposed mediation hypotheses. Survey data were collected from 360 students across three higher vocational colleges in Shandong Province, China. Using mediation analysis, results show that both teacher support and parental support significantly predict academic performance. Learning engagement partially mediates the relationships between teacher support and academic performance, and between parental support and academic performance, indicating that external support improves outcomes partly by strengthening students’ behavioural, emotional, and cognitive engagement in learning. Overall, the findings highlight learning engagement as a practical lever for enhancing performance in higher vocational education. Findings suggest strengthening home–school collaboration and implementing engagement-focused teaching strategies (e.g., supportive classroom interactions and autonomy-supportive practices) to increase learning engagement and improve academic performance.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Education: Opportunities, Challenges, and the Future of Learning in Developing Countries: A Bangladesh-Focused Systematic Critical Literature Review and the Socio-Technical AI Integration Framework (STAIF)
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming education through personalized learning, intelligent tutoring, automated assessment, learning analytics, teacher support, and generative AI applications. However, the benefits of AI are not distributed equally, particularly in developing countries where digital infrastructure, teacher readiness, affordability, data governance, language diversity, and institutional capacity remain significant challenges. This study critically examines the opportunities, challenges, and future implications of AI in education, with particular attention to developing-country contexts and Bangladesh. A PRISMA-informed Systematic Critical Literature Review (SCLR) was conducted using peer-reviewed research, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and authoritative institutional reports published primarily between 2018 and 2026. The review synthesizes evidence concerning personalized learning, teacher augmentation, generative AI, assessment, academic integrity, AI literacy, digital inequality, privacy, bias, and contextual adaptation. Bangladesh-specific evidence is incorporated to examine the country's readiness and the practical requirements for responsible AI adoption in education. The review indicates that AI can improve personalization, student engagement, feedback, learning efficiency, teacher productivity, and access to educational support. Recent experimental evidence also suggests that generative AI can produce positive learning effects when integrated with appropriate instructional design. Nevertheless, these benefits depend heavily on teacher involvement, infrastructure, institutional governance, and responsible implementation. Risks include misinformation, academic dishonesty, algorithmic bias, privacy violations, overreliance on automated systems, unequal access, and the marginalization of local languages and cultures. Based on the synthesis, this study proposes the Socio-Technical AI Integration Framework (STAIF), consisting of seven interconnected pillars: infrastructure-first deployment, teacher-in-the-loop implementation, local-language and cultural adaptation, offline-first accessibility, equity safeguards, responsible data governance, and continuous monitoring and evaluation. The framework provides a practical pathway for developing countries such as Bangladesh to move from fragmented AI experimentation toward equitable, sustainable, and human-centred AI integration in education.

items.title: The paradox of pleasing: therapeutic recognition and the limits of conversational AI
items.abstract: Abstract Conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) is increasingly used by hundreds of millions of people for emotional support, personal advice, and therapeutic purposes, rapidly emerging as a mediator of human self-understanding (Stade et al. 2025). Yet despite growing evidence of systematic user-validation in CAI, documented as “sycophancy” in the AI safety literature (Sharma et al. 2024), its implications for how individuals come to understand themselves remain largely unexamined. This article addresses that gap by reframing sycophancy not as a technical alignment failure or a purely philosophical concern, but as a failure of recognition in the psychoanalytic and critical-theoretical sense. We identify a core tension we term the “paradox of pleasing”: CAI’s drive to please renders it structurally unable to provide the friction, conflict, and encounter with otherness that genuine recognition requires. Drawing on Winnicott’s (1960, 1971) concepts of “holding” and “object use,” we contend that CAI’s inability to provide necessary resistance or survive aggression prevents the transformative psychological development found in the human therapeutic encounter. Extending this analysis through Honneth’s (1995) theory of recognition and Whitebook’s (2001a, 2021) critique of Honneth, we argue that CAI reflects the undervaluing of the “work of the negative.” This limitation risks flattening consciousness by converting collective political frustration into privatized, soothed affect, undermining the conditions for critical social thought. The article concludes by suggesting that the encounter with the paradox of pleasing ultimately serves to foreground the unique and indispensable nature of human therapeutic recognition.

items.title: Trust in AI Versus Human Clinicians: A Study of Diagnostic Judgements and Transparency
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being considered for use in healthcare, including clinical diagnosis, with potential to support clinicians and address pressures on healthcare systems. However, public trust remains an important consideration in the adoption of AI-based clinical decision-making. This study investigated perceptions of and trust in AI and human clinicians, particularly when their diagnostic judgements were either consistent or conflicting. The study also explored whether concerns regarding transparency and liability influenced preferences for medical AI.Methods: An experimental vignette and questionnaire-based study was conducted to examine participants' responses to diagnostic judgements made by AI and human clinicians. Vignettes presented scenarios in which AI and human clinicians provided either the same or conflicting diagnostic judgements. Participants' levels of trust and preferences regarding medical AI were assessed, alongside their concerns about transparency and liability.Results: Participants demonstrated greater trust in human clinicians than in AI clinicians. However, agreement between AI and human clinicians' diagnostic judgements was associated with increased trust in the resulting diagnosis. Participants who expressed greater concern about transparency reported lower levels of trust in medical AI. The findings therefore indicate that perceptions of AI-based diagnosis may be influenced not only by whether the diagnosis is consistent with that of a human clinician, but also by concerns surrounding transparency and accountability.Conclusions: Trust in AI-based clinical diagnosis appears to remain lower than trust in human clinicians, although agreement between human and AI diagnostic judgements may increase confidence in AI-supported decisions. Concerns regarding transparency may represent an important barrier to trust and acceptance. Developing transparent standards and clearly communicating how AI-based clinical decisions are generated and governed may therefore be important considerations in the adoption of medical AI.

items.title: Understanding Public Trust in AI-Based Clinical Psychological Decision-Making: A Qualitative Study
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied within healthcare and has the potential to support clinical decision-making and improve the efficiency of healthcare delivery. However, concerns surrounding the use of AI in healthcare may influence public trust in AI-generated diagnoses and treatment decisions. These concerns may be particularly important within clinical psychological settings, where decisions can involve sensitive personal information and significant implications for patients.Methods: This qualitative study explored factors influencing public trust in AI-based decision-making within a clinical psychological context. In-depth semi-structured interviews were conducted to explore participants' perceptions of AI and the factors that may influence their willingness to trust AI-generated decisions. Interview data were analysed using deductive thematic analysis. Particular attention was given to perceptions of transparency, system design, bias, privacy, regulation, and responsibility. Participants' perspectives on AI functioning as an assistant to a healthcare professional compared with AI operating as an independent decision-making tool were also explored.Results: Several factors were identified as influencing trust in AI-based clinical psychological decision-making, including transparency, system design, perceived bias, privacy, regulation, and responsibility for AI-generated decisions. Participants also distinguished between AI used as an assistant to healthcare professionals and AI operating independently, indicating that the perceived role and level of human involvement may influence trust in AI decisions. Clear ethical and legal frameworks may further support public confidence in the responsible use of AI in clinical decision-making.

items.title: When caring depletes: the paradox of leading employee wellbeing during a prolonged crisis – evidence from the Australian resources sector
items.abstract: Purpose The protracted COVID-19 crisis placed substantial demands on managers in the Australian resources industry. While workers' wellbeing received increased attention during this period, much less is known about how managers sustained their own wellbeing while providing care, reassurance, and operational continuity. Drawing on the JD–R model, paradox theory, and moral strain perspectives, we examine wellbeing-oriented leadership during a sustained crisis. We focus on how leadership behaviour operated as both a resource for employees and a demand on managers, shaping their own wellbeing experiences and leadership identity. Design/methodology/approach An interpretative phenomenological approach (IPA) was employed. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 32 managers in the Australian mining, oil, and gas sector. The interview accounts were analysed using IPA to examine how participants made sense of responsibility, care, and uncertainty during a prolonged crisis. Findings The findings indicate that leadership during a prolonged crisis embodied a Demand–Resource Paradox (DRP). Practices such as emotional support, constant availability, and responsibility for safety and wellbeing decisions acted as resources for employees while imposing demands on managers. Sustained over time, these practices contributed to the accumulation of psychological strain and resource depletion. Originality/value First, we extend JD–R theory by identifying a Demand–Resource Paradox in which wellbeing-oriented leadership supports workers while depleting managers. Second, we advance moral strain research by showing how moral strain accumulates through prolonged crisis-related responsibility. Third, we reconceptualise crisis leadership as an endurance-based process, distinct from resilience models, by emphasising chronic demands, cumulative depletion, identity reshaping, and the absence of clear recovery periods.

items.title: Workplace Ergonomics and Employees’ Performance: The Moderating Effect of Job Satisfaction in Microfinance Institutions of Bamenda, Cameroon
items.abstract: The purpose of this study is to investigate the effect of workplace ergonomics on employees’ performance while assessing the moderating role of job satisfaction in microfinance institutions (MFIs) of Bamenda, Cameroon. Physical ergonomics, cognitive ergonomics and organisational ergonomics are used to measure workplace ergonomics. The study adopts a quantitative-causal research design with the use of questionnaires administered to 140 employees in MFIs in Bamenda, Cameroon. The Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Technique is used to analyse the data collected. The results show that physical ergonomics has a positive (0.136) and significant effect on employees’ performance, cognitive ergonomics has a positive (0.509) and significant effect on employee performance and organisational ergonomics also has a positive (0.111) and significant effect on employees’ performance. On the other hand, job satisfaction has a positive (0.387) significant moderating effect on the relationship between physical ergonomics and employees’ performance, but not for cognitive ergonomics and organisational ergonomics. MFIs should prioritise investments in physical workplace improvements such as ergonomic furniture, proper lighting, and comfortable workspaces to promote better employee performance. To improve on cognitive ergonomics, MFIs should create training programs aimed at improving cognitive ergonomics to enhance employees’ mental processes and decision-making skills, ultimately leading to higher performance levels. MFIs and other organisations should evaluate their internal processes and structures to ensure they are conducive to optimise employee performance.

items.title: Human Factors in Construction Risk Management
items.abstract: This research aims to explore the key human factors relevant to construction risk management and their effects on risk management outcomes. It primarily focuses on how communication, leadership style, experience and training, team dynamics, cognitive biases, stress and fatigue, and safety culture influence outcomes on the construction site. There has been much advancement of technology and implementation of safety measures; nevertheless, human behavior still plays an important role in contributing to accidents in the construction industry. The literature review and analysis of previous studies relevant to the research provided an insight into crucial human factors that affect risk perception and risk management. The research was quantitative and included an anonymous survey completed by 141 workers in the construction sector. The results suggest that good communication skills, supportive leadership, ongoing practices, good team dynamics, cognitive biases, stress and fatigue, and safety culture are all important to consider when implementing safety management systems. The research recommends that the practical strategies of key human factors be built into the current risk management systems, which can further improve safety and reduce construction site accidents. In addition, this study advocates for improved construction settings that enable a proactive response to risk management across the construction sector.

items.title: Questionnaire Design and Rater Cognition in 360-Degree Performance Appraisal
items.abstract: Questionnaire design may play an important yet underexamined role in shaping the quality of performance appraisal data. This study examines whether redesigning response formats in a 360-degree feedback system is associated with improvements in rating behavior, response quality, and psychometric consistency. Drawing on cognitive processing and response-process perspectives, we compare a traditional numeric Likert-format questionnaire with a redesigned format incorporating behaviorally descriptive response options, modified visual presentation, and variable response ordering. Data were collected across two appraisal periods within a large production organization employing more than 25,000 individuals. A total of 26,672 questionnaires were distributed, and 18,621 responses were obtained for the evaluation of approximately 900 managers in different levels. Following the redesign, participation rates increased from 47% to 79%, and internal consistency reliability improved from Cronbach’s α = 0.902 to α = 0.939. Response distributions also became less concentrated in extreme categories and more evenly distributed across intermediate categories, indicating greater rating differentiation and reduced response bias. These findings are consistent with the argument that behaviorally descriptive response formats encourage greater cognitive engagement and reduce reliance on heuristic responding during performance evaluation. The study contributes to performance appraisal and multisource feedback research by highlighting the role of questionnaire design in shaping response processes, rating behavior, and measurement quality. Together, the findings provide evidence compatible with the view that relatively small and scalable questionnaire design modifications may enhance cognitive engagement, improve measurement quality, and increase the validity and practical usefulness of organizational appraisal data.

items.title: Heuristics for managing rework-related safety risks in construction: An ecological rationality approach
items.abstract: Rework during construction often heightens exposure to safety incidents. It frequently stems from decisions made under epistemic uncertainty, when incomplete knowledge of design, site conditions, or task interactions leads to outcomes that require later correction. These situations involve complex human, organizational, and technical interactions whose causal mechanisms are only partially understood and difficult to quantify. As a result, probabilistic and optimization-based risk models can be difficult to operationalize because the information needed to estimate reliable probabilities is often incomplete, inconsistent, and not transferable across project contexts. Using an interpretive case study and retrospective sense-making as analytical lenses, smart heuristics grounded in ecological rationality are developed to support stop–verify–proceed, isolate–stabilize, and escalation decisions when non-conformances pose safety risks in an AU$19.8 billion transport project. Drawing on documented rework events in construction, several Fast-and-Frugal Trees—a smart heuristic—are presented alongside simple, cue-based decision rules as structured decision templates that can support explicit, traceable decision-making and provide a basis for future empirical evaluation. The proposed smart heuristics translate tacit field experience into explicit, communicable decision structures to assist practitioners in structuring their judgment when information is incomplete and time for analysis is limited. By operationalizing bounded rationality through practical heuristic tools, our paper advances understanding of decision-making under uncertainty in construction and demonstrates a systematic approach for structuring quality management information into heuristic decision pathways that can inform future safety risk management.

items.title: Large-scale experimental study of stair evacuation speeds for heterogeneous individuals in high-rise buildings
items.abstract: Accurate characterization of stair evacuation speeds in high-rise buildings is essential for evacuation modelling and safety design involving heterogeneous populations. This study reports a large-scale evacuation experiment involving 1,249 participants aged 6–82 years in a 27-storey residential building. Participants descended stairs individually, allowing the effects of physiological and demographic attributes on unimpeded evacuation performance to be isolated from crowd interactions and density effects. Overall average evacuation speeds, floor-by-floor speed profiles, and speed reduction rates during evacuation process were quantified. Age was the dominant determinant of evacuation speed. Evacuation speed increased rapidly between 6–20 years of age, remained relatively stable between 21–60 years, and declined markedly thereafter. Beyond conventional single-factor analysis, this study examined the interacting effects of demographic and physiological attributes on evacuation speed. The largest gender difference occurred among participants aged 11–20 years, whereas no significant gender difference was observed among those aged > 60 years under the current sample. BMI category significantly affected evacuation speed only among male children aged 6–10 years but influenced a broader age range (6–50 years) among female participants. Participants with postgraduate education exhibited significantly lower evacuation speeds than those with other educational attainments. A linear mixed-effects model further identified significant effects of evacuation distance, age, gender, and BMI category on speed reduction during prolonged stair descent. This study provides a comprehensive dataset of stair evacuation performance across the lifespan and reveals new insights into attribute-dependent evacuation performance, supporting refinement of fire safety design parameters and calibration of evacuation models for high-rise buildings.

items.title: Leisure under lock: cognitive activation and motivation erosion as mechanisms undermining experiential quality of leisure time
items.abstract: Most people switch between work and nonwork roles daily. Past research shows that work stressors can impair micro-role transitions from work to nonwork by activating work-related cognitions. However, motivational processes may be equally important for understanding why psychologically transitioning into nonwork roles fails. Therefore, we examine motivation erosion (i.e. reduced leisure-related self-efficacy) alongside cognitive activation (i.e. increased negative work prospection) as parallel processes interfering with successful transitioning from the work role to nonwork roles. Accordingly, in a preregistered 14-day diary study with morning and after-work measurements, we examined the effects of daily unfinished tasks and anticipated workload on evening experiential quality of leisure time (i.e. the extent to which free time is pleasurable, meaningful, and engaging) via increased negative work prospection and diminished leisure-related self-efficacy. In addition, we tested job involvement, trait mindfulness, and psychological flexibility as cross-level moderators. Dynamic multilevel structural equation model path results (N = 179, n = 1,849) support all hypotheses. Additionally, we found that psychological flexibility offsets the negative effect of unfinished tasks on leisure-related self-efficacy. Our findings highlight that work demands spilling over into nonwork time affects leisure time experiences, impacting daily quality of life through a cognitive, as well as a motivational mechanism.
